Split-horizon DNS and PrivateLink interface endpoints

transcript: [00:00] Sofia Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to deep dive into the private vpc setup and esp the egress and dns behavior you saw in the earlier perf runs.

[00:18] Dana Rivers: Hi Sofia, thanks. Short context: our staging runs showed intermittent 95th percentile spikes when the KV cache misses and when some requests hit an external resolver through a nat gateway. We wanted to understand if it's the runtime or networking.

[00:34] Marcus Patel: got it. quick note — we generally see two separate sources of tail latency: model runtime (kv cache cold misses, decoder kv thrash) and network egress (dns, private link fallbacks). we'll walk through both and then propose tests.

[01:01] Owen Park: the team uses a nat-gateway currently in the shared-services account, and we have interface privatelink endpoints for s3 and secrets. our resolver is the vpc resolver in each subnet, forwarded to a central dns fleet.
[01:25] Iris López: small clarification — are you using AWS Route 53 Resolver endpoints with outbound endpoints? that changes whether the dns goes across the nat or over the privatelink interface.
[01:42] Owen Park: yes outbound endpoints, forwarded to their corporate resolver. so dns ends up leaving the vpc in some paths.

[01:55] Marcus Patel: that can add 20-150ms per call in our experience when the resolver path forces an egress hop. especially when the model runtime issues many small lookups (e.g., dynamic prompt templating hitting a config service).

[02:14] Priya Nair: right — security requires that corporate resolver for blocklisting. but we can consider splitting internal service records into a split-horizon zone with Route53 private hosted zones.

[02:30] Sofia Chen: quick agenda: 1) show where latency comes from (network vs runtime), 2) KV cache patterns and mitigation (prefetching, prefix caching), 3) network recommendations (privatelink, nat instance tuning, mtu), 4) next steps.

[03:00] Marcus Patel: starting with runtime: our serving runtime keeps a KV cache per model shard. cold requests that need to fetch large KV pages or have uncommon prefixes can cause synchronous reads which block token generation and inflate p95.
[03:22] Leo Martins: is the KV cache local to the GPU node or a shared redis? we currently point to an internal memcached cluster.

[03:31] Marcus Patel: in Redwood private deployments we recommend local, memory-backed kv cache colocated with the inference process for the tightest latency. external caches add network hops and jitter. memcached can be okay but you see network variance.
[03:51] Dana Rivers: ok — we're using memcached because our infra team wanted centralized control. can we quantify the difference?

[04:03] Marcus Patel: rough numbers from our benchmarks: local-memory kv hit path ~0.8-2 ms per token; external memcached in same AZ ~5-12 ms depending on load; cross-AZ or through nat/resolver paths adds 20-60ms. those are ballpark p50 numbers for small keys.
[04:26] Owen Park: interesting — our p95 spikes were ~180-200ms for some requests, which aligns with cross-AZ plus resolver delays.
[04:39] Iris López: also consider batching: if you can batch short requests you amortize KV overhead. but for latency-sensitive routes (1-2 token prompts) batching may not help.

[04:55] Marcus Patel: yes — continuous batching in the runtime groups requests and reduces per-token kernel overhead, but only when you have concurrency. We saw ~2-3x throughput improvement with batching but tail latency can still suffer if some requests depend on remote services before enqueuing.
[05:20] Priya Nair: on the networking side, why would DNS add 100ms? doesn't DNS cache in the resolver?

[05:28] Marcus Patel: it normally does, but if you have an outbound forwarding chain to corporate DNS, you might hit cold or TTL-expired entries. Also split-horizon setups with PrivateLink sometimes require conditional forwarding to an endpoint that is behind an armored firewall, adding hops.
[05:48] Dana Rivers: we also saw TCP retransmits when large responses traversed a nat instance with MTU mismatch — can that affect token latency?

[05:58] Marcus Patel: yes — MTU mismatches cause fragmentation or retransmits which hurt latency for larger payloads, like embeddings or multi-token responses. we recommend validating MTU end-to-end; for AWS ENIs default 9001 (jumbo) can help if supported across the path.
[06:22] Leo Martins: about PrivateLink — we configured interface endpoints for S3 and Secrets Manager. do you recommend adding an interface endpoint for the Redwood control plane or inference nodes?

[06:35] Sofia Chen: we can do interface endpoints for the control plane services (private control plane). For inference egress, the trick is ensuring data plane traffic stays within the VPC or via VPC peering — avoid private link that forces additional dns lookups unless using VPC endpoint-specific hostnames.

[06:58] Marcus Patel: when using PrivateLink, Route53 resolvers sometimes return the endpoint's regional hostname which is fine, but if your resolver forwards to a corporate resolver that rewrites names you may get unexpected public egress. We frequently see misconfigured forwarding rules.
[07:18] Owen Park: any immediate remediation we can test?

[07:22] Marcus Patel: simplest: create a Route53 private hosted zone for your redwood service FQNs and point them to the interface endpoint IPs. That prevents the outbound chain. Also adjust DNS TTLs and ensure resolvers are caching.
[07:40] Dana Rivers: we can do that. what about NAT Gateway vs NAT instance? our current approach is NAT Gateway but cost is high, and we wondered if nat-instance would reduce variance.

[07:53] Marcus Patel: NAT Gateway is managed and scales; it generally has lower jitter than a tiny NAT instance but you can still see bursts depending on underlying hardware. NAT instances are tunable (you can size, enable enhanced networking, tune iptables) but require management. For p95 reduction, a well-provisioned NAT instance in each AZ with placement groups can actually reduce cross-AZ hops.
[08:18] Iris López: we usually recommend localized egress per AZ to avoid cross-AZ charges and variability. Route tables should point subnets to an AZ-local NAT path.
[08:30] Priya Nair: security: any implications for KMS or HSM calls from nodes when private? we call KMS during model loading for encrypted checkpoints.

[08:38] Marcus Patel: KMS calls add an external network hop. For lower latency, use VPC endpoints for KMS/SecretsManager and keep endpoints private. Also, cache decrypted keys in memory for session duration rather than re-requesting KMS on every model shard load.
[08:57] Leo Martins: good tip — we had KMS calls per shard reload which was causing stalls during autoscaling.
[09:06] Dana Rivers: on quantization: does lower-bit quantization change network patterns? we plan to use 8-bit quant for cost.

[09:14] Marcus Patel: quantization primarily changes compute and memory footprint; it can reduce memory pressure and thus reduce swap or paging which indirectly reduces network calls for spilling. It doesn't directly change DNS or egress patterns, but with denser models you might be able to colocate more shards per host which reduces cross-host fetches.

[09:36] Sofia Chen: circling back to KV cache: two immediate mitigations — pre-warming with representative prompts and enabling prefix caching in the runtime. prefix caching stores common prompt prefixes so the KV hits are much higher for repeatable flows.
[09:55] Marcus Patel: concretely, enabling prefix caching bumped hit rate from ~78% to ~95% in a customer with many templated prompts; that moved p95 from ~220ms to ~90ms on their critical route.
[10:12] Owen Park: how invasive is prefix caching to our app code?
[10:18] Iris López: minimal — it's a runtime config and optionally you provide a small prompt corpus to seed the cache. no code changes required unless you want custom TTL rules.
[10:31] Dana Rivers: what about the startup cold cache problem during deploys or scale-outs?

[10:36] Marcus Patel: for scale-outs we recommend a warmup job that runs synthetic requests to populate the KV cache and model warm paths before routing production traffic. Redwood Optimize can orchestrate warmups during canary rollouts.
[10:51] Leah (background voice, mislabeled as "Speaker 5"): can you also look at the tcp keepalives? we saw ephemeral connection churn.

[10:59] Marcus Patel: yes — keepalives, connection pooling and reuse are critical. Short-lived connections to external caches or DNS cause extra TLS handshakes which add tens of ms. Use connection reuse and prefer in-AZ endpoints.
[11:18] Priya Nair: any notes about entropy or randomization that could cause cache mis-hits? our app stamps trace IDs onto prompts and we've struggled with low cache hit rates.

[11:29] Marcus Patel: telemetry/tracing injected into the prompt body can indeed defeat prefix caching. Recommend separating tracing metadata from the textual prompt or use a stable prompt template with metadata in headers if the runtime supports it.
[11:45] Sofia Chen: network diagnostics: we'll need traceroutes, tcpdump captures, and dns logs from your staging run. Owen, can your team collect that for the two benchmark windows Marcus described?
[11:58] Owen Park: yes — we can do two windows: 1) existing config, 2) with route53 private zone and nat-instance in one AZ. we'll capture p50/p95, kernel drops, and tcp retransmits.

[12:12] Marcus Patel: great. for the perf test we propose three vectors: a) KV-cache hit path microbench (single tokens, measure token latency), b) batch throughput test (high concurrency), c) end-to-end inference including DNS and external calls. We can provide a test harness.
[12:28] Dana Rivers: will the test harness require privileged access or any creds?

[12:33] Marcus Patel: minimal creds to hit the inference endpoints; we'll provide CloudFormation for the harness to run inside your account. no secrets should be sent to Redwood; instrumented metrics can be exported to a S3 bucket or CloudWatch.
[12:47] Iris López: plus we'll include a small script to pre-warm prefixes using representative prompt traces you share (anonymized).
[12:57] Dana Rivers: on the DNS side, we want a checklist — who owns what changes in our infra?

[13:03] Sofia Chen: Redwood can provide the checklist. typical steps: create private hosted zone, add A records for endpoint FQNs, ensure resolver rules don't forward those to corporate resolver, validate TTL and caching, and run a resolver health test.
[13:20] Priya Nair: what about egress logs for audits? we need those for SOC2 evidence.
[13:26] Marcus Patel: enable VPC flow logs to a central logging account and also capture Route53 query logs — both are useful for audit trails and for diagnosing intermittent egress.
[13:38] Leo Martins: any example numbers for throughput and cost that we can use for capacity planning?

[13:44] Marcus Patel: example: a medium gpt-3 style model at 8-bit quant on a single A100-equivalent node can serve ~150 tokens/sec baseline with batching; with continuous batching and optimized kernels throughput jumps to 400-600 tokens/sec. cost depends on instance pricing and egress — NAT Gateway cost per GB can add up, so local egress reduces cost.
[14:06] Dana Rivers: good — helps make the procurement case. one more question: if a model fallback to hosted is configured, does that change the data path for private deployments?

[14:16] Marcus Patel: yes — fallback to hosted will cause egress to Redwood's hosted endpoints, which should be covered in the network design and compliance docs. For strict air-gapped customers we recommend disabling automatic fallback and using local model variants for failover.

[14:34] Sofia Chen: ok let's recap quickly. Action items: Marcus will run perf harness and share spreadsheet comparing nat-gateway vs nat-instance; Owen will share subnet/route table diagrams and run traceroutes; Sofia will send PrivateLink and Route53 checklist and CloudFormation snippets; Priya will collate compliance doc needs. We schedule follow-up on 2025-12-11.
[14:58] Owen Park: one quick miscellaneous: we've had issues with ephemeral ephemeral ephemeral ip allocations on interface endpoints — any tips?
[15:06] Marcus Patel: ensure you reserve enough private DNS hostnames and consider ENI warm pools. Also monitor interface endpoint quotas per AZ and request increases early.
[15:20] Dana Rivers: thanks everyone. we'll start the data capture tomorrow and aim to have results next week.
[15:27] Sofia Chen: excellent. we'll share the test harness and configs shortly. thanks all — talk soon.
[15:35] [call end]
